name: Ritlecitinib (Litfulo)
lead: Ritlecitinib, sold as Litfulo and developed by Pfizer, is an oral kinase inhibitor prescribed for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, in adults and adolescents aged 12 and older.[1][2] The US label describes it as irreversibly inhibiting Janus kinase 3 (JAK3) and the TEC family of kinases, and notes that the relevance of inhibiting specific enzymes to its therapeutic effect is not currently known.[1]

It was first approved by the US FDA in June 2023, followed by the European Union in September 2023 and Canada in November 2023.[2][3] It is a prescription-only drug and is not indicated for androgenetic (pattern) hair loss, the form of hair loss most discussed in looksmaxxing communities.[1] Its label carries a boxed warning covering serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1]

For people with alopecia areata, the visible payoff is regrowth of hair lost in patches or across the whole scalp, and in some cases the face and body. In the pivotal trial, the main outcome was a Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) score of 20 or less, meaning at most about a fifth of the scalp still bare, measured at 24 weeks. [13]

paras: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system targets hair follicles, causing non-scarring loss of scalp, face or body hair. It can progress to complete scalp loss (alopecia totalis) or loss of all body hair (alopecia universalis). [12] A European expert consensus statement notes that hair loss affects quality of life and that children and adolescents with the condition often experience bullying. [12]

Severity is scored with SALT or the Alopecia Areata Scale; a SALT score of 20 or more is commonly accepted as an indication to consider systemic therapy. [12] The consensus lists baricitinib for adults and ritlecitinib for people aged 12 and older as the only two EMA-approved medicines for severe disease, with glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, methotrexate and azathioprine used off-label, and oral minoxidil considered an adjunct with limited data. [12]
This is different from pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia), the type most discussed in looksmaxxing communities; ritlecitinib is not indicated for it. [1]

The US label lists severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents 12 years and older as the indication. It states that use together with other JAK inhibitors, biologic immunomodulators, cyclosporine or other potent immunosuppressants is not recommended.[1]

Beyond alopecia areata, registered studies have explored ritlecitinib in non-segmental vitiligo (a phase 3 programme), keloids, chronic spontaneous urticaria and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; these are investigational uses.[4][5][6][7]

Per the label, ritlecitinib binds irreversibly at the ATP-binding site of JAK3 and of the TEC kinase family, blocking cytokine-induced STAT phosphorylation mediated by JAK3-dependent receptors and signalling by TEC-dependent immune receptors.[1] Grokipedia describes the drug as sparing other Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, TYK2) in biochemical assays and reducing cytotoxic activity of natural killer cells and CD8 T cells, which it connects with hair regrowth; that source is AI-generated and should be read with caution.[8]
Grokipedia reports rapid oral absorption with peak levels in about an hour and a terminal half-life of roughly 1.3 to 2.3 hours.[8]

The most common adverse reactions listed on the label (incidence 1% or more) include headache, diarrhea, acne, rash, urticaria, folliculitis, fever, atopic dermatitis and dizziness.[1] The boxed warning describes increased risk of serious bacterial, fungal, viral and opportunistic infections including tuberculosis, along with mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1]

Warnings and precautions also cover hypersensitivity, hypoglycemia in people with diabetes, laboratory abnormalities (lymphocyte and platelet counts to be checked before starting) and avoidance of live vaccines.[1] The label states that animal studies caused fetotoxicity and malformations at high exposures and that human pregnancy data are insufficient; a pregnancy exposure registry exists.[1]

Approval rested on the ALLEGRO programme, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b/3 trial (NCT03732807) in about 718 participants aged 12 and over with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss, run at 128 sites in 18 countries.[3] Grokipedia states that the trial showed significantly greater scalp hair coverage than placebo at 24 weeks.[8]

In the Lancet report of ALLEGRO phase 2b/3, the share of patients reaching SALT 20 or less (no more than about a fifth of the scalp affected) at week 24 ranged from 14% to 31% across the four main ritlecitinib regimens, compared with 2% on placebo, and every comparison with placebo was statistically significant. Adverse events through week 48 occurred in roughly 76% to 86% of patients across arms, were similar in incidence between groups, and there were no deaths. [13]

In the ALLEGRO-LT long-term extension, reported in 2025, the 449 patients who began ritlecitinib at study entry had an average exposure of about 729 days; at month 24, about 74% had SALT 20 or less and about 66% had SALT 10 or less (as-observed analysis), and eyebrow and eyelash response rates were about 61% and 66%. [15] Around 86% reported treatment-emergent adverse events, most mild or moderate, the commonest being positive COVID-19 tests, headache and fever; serious adverse events occurred in 4.9%, and herpes zoster, serious infections, malignancies and major cardiovascular events were each reported in small numbers of patients. [15]

Later registrations include real-world retrospective studies in US patients with severe alopecia areata and phase 3 work in vitiligo.[9][10][5] Several phase 1 pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers have also been registered.[11] No published trial has examined ritlecitinib for androgenetic alopecia.

The Lancet report of the phase 2b-3 trial randomised patients aged 12 and older with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss to once-daily ritlecitinib or placebo for 24 weeks at 118 sites in 18 countries, with several dose arms including a 4-week loading dose, followed by a 24-week extension in which placebo patients switched to ritlecitinib. [13]

A separate analysis reported results in the adolescent subgroup, and an open-label long-term study (ALLEGRO-LT) followed adults and adolescents with at least 25 percent scalp hair loss. [14][15] In vitiligo, a phase 2b trial in active nonsegmental disease has been published and a phase 3 programme is ongoing. [16]

Pfizer developed ritlecitinib under the code PF-06651600. A phase 2a study compared it and another JAK inhibitor, brepocitinib, in alopecia areata over 24 weeks. [17] The phase 2b/3 ALLEGRO trial followed, and the FDA approved the drug in June 2023, the European Union in September 2023 and Canada in November 2023. [3][18]

A review in the journal Drugs described it as the first approval of a JAK3/TEC inhibitor for alopecia areata, an orally given capsule that is taken daily. [18] Wikipedia lists an annual US list price of about 49,000 US dollars. [3]

Reviews describe JAK inhibitors as changing the outlook for moderate-to-severe alopecia areata, which had previously been difficult to treat. [20][19] Ritlecitinib differs from baricitinib in being selective for JAK3 and the TEC family rather than JAK1 and JAK2, and it is approved down to age 12. [12]

Because treatment is for an immune-mediated disease, dermatologists assess severity, history and laboratory results before prescribing, and the label calls for checks such as lymphocyte and platelet counts. [1]

Dermatologists also weigh the label's boxed warning about infections, malignancy and cardiovascular events against the burden of disease, and the consensus statement frames systemic therapy as for severe or persistent cases. [1][12]

Ritlecitinib is marketed by Pfizer as Litfulo, a daily oral capsule, and is the second JAK inhibitor approved for alopecia areata after baricitinib. [3][18] Wikipedia lists an annual US list price of about 49,000 US dollars. [3] A European expert consensus statement lists it among the systemic options for severe disease. [12]

For people living with alopecia areata, regrowth of scalp, eyebrow and eyelash hair is the visible outcome measured in trials, and registry and patient-reported outcomes such as the Patient Global Impression of Change are used alongside SALT scores. [15] Because the drug requires a prescription and laboratory monitoring, it sits in clinical dermatology rather than in over-the-counter hair-loss discussions. [1]

card.summary: Prescription JAK3 inhibitor for severe alopecia areata, not for pattern baldness, and with a boxed warning.
card.note: Approved only for severe alopecia areata; boxed warning for infections, malignancy, cardiovascular events and thrombosis.

quick.overview:
Ritlecitinib (Litfulo) is a daily pill from Pfizer approved in 2023 for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair loss condition, in people 12 and older.

It is not approved for ordinary male or female pattern hair loss, and no published trial has tested it there, so its relevance to cosmetic hair goals is limited.
quick.mechanism: It irreversibly blocks JAK3 and TEC-family kinases, dampening immune signalling involved in the attack on hair follicles, although the label says the importance of each target to its effect is not known.
quick.risks: The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major cardiovascular events and thrombosis. Common effects include headache, diarrhea and acne. It is prescription only and reportedly costs about US$49,000 a year.
